summary: This bill amends patent law to require a patent owner's consent before any petition for inter partes review or post-grant review can be filed.

scores.thoughts: The bill amends patent law to require patent owner consent for inter partes or post-grant review petitions. It contains no provisions related to federal spending, appropriations, or budgets.
The bill makes changes only to patent review procedures under Title 35. It has no tax-related provisions or implications.
While patents can indirectly affect pharmaceuticals, the bill addresses only procedural consent requirements for patent challenges and does not engage with healthcare policy, coverage, or markets.
The bill is limited to patent administrative procedures and has no connection to firearms or gun regulations.
No provisions in the bill address immigration, visas, borders, or related protections.
The bill contains nothing related to reproductive rights or abortion access.
The legislation does not address military, defense, or national security spending or policy.
No environmental regulations, climate provisions, or energy policy appear in the bill.
The bill does not touch welfare programs, entitlements, or social safety net policies.
Patent procedure changes have no bearing on schools, education funding, or school choice.
The bill makes no changes to drug enforcement, decriminalization, or controlled substances policy.
No provisions relate to sentencing, policing, rehabilitation, or criminal procedure.
Although patents are a form of intellectual property, the bill's narrow procedural change does not engage with trade agreements, tariffs, or globalization.
The bill has no fiscal impact, deficit provisions, or debt-related measures.
The legislation contains no civil rights, anti-discrimination, or LGBTQ-related provisions.
No foreign aid, international assistance, or diplomatic provisions are present.
The bill does not address voting rights, election integrity, or electoral procedures.
While patents often involve technology, the bill only alters review consent rules and does not regulate technology companies, data privacy, or oversight.
No labor, employment, or union-related content exists in the bill.
The bill does not engage with religious exemptions, civil rights, or anti-discrimination law.
